Non-UKAEA employees who are affected by or involved in a complaint are encouraged to contact their own employer for access to support services or resources available to them.

Anyone who raises a complaint or participates in good faith in a bullying or harassment investigation must not experience any form of detrimental treatment or victimisation. If an employee believes they have been treated unfairly as a result of raising or participating in such a matter, they should inform their line manager or the People and Culture team as soon as possible.

Regardless of the outcome of a complaint, UKAEA will carefully consider how best to manage any ongoing working relationship between the individuals involved, including any third parties. This may include, where appropriate, adjustments to job duties, work location, or reporting lines, or the offer of workplace mediation to help rebuild a positive and respectful working environment.

Employees who require time away from work relating to a complaint of bullying, harassment or sexual harassment should discuss this with their line manager or, where the concern involves their line manager, an alternative manager or the People & Culture Team. Requests for annual leave or sickness absence will be managed in line with the Absences & Leave Policy and Sickness Absence Policy, as appropriate.

8.4 Sensitivity and confidentiality

Confidentiality, and trust in that confidentiality, is essential when handling allegations of inappropriate behaviour. All individuals involved in an informal or formal complaint process concerning harassment, sexual harassment, bullying, discrimination, or victimisation, including complainants, respondents, witnesses, and those supporting the process, are required to maintain strict confidentiality at all times.

Information relating to a complaint, including the identities of the individuals concerned, must only be shared on a genuine “need-to-know” basis and only with those who are formally involved in managing or investigating the matter. This requirement is in place to protect the integrity of the process, uphold fairness, and safeguard the dignity and wellbeing of all parties.

Breaches of confidentiality, or behaviour that demonstrates a lack of sensitivity, professionalism, or respect for the process, will be treated seriously. For employees, this may result in disciplinary action, up to and including dismissal. For non-employees (such as contractors, agency workers, or visitors), other appropriate action may be taken, which could include termination of engagement or removal of access to the workplace.

8.5 Malicious or vexatious complaints

A malicious complaint is one that is made with the intention to intimidate, to lower the reputation of, or otherwise injure or harm somebody, through knowingly providing false or misleading information or withholding information about an incident or issue.

A vexatious complaint is either one that is made with the sole or main intention to harass, annoy or subdue somebody, or one that is unreasonable, without foundation, frivolous, repetitive, deliberately burdensome or unwarranted.

Making a malicious or vexatious complaint is regarded as misconduct and may result in disciplinary action, up to and including summary dismissal.

UKAEA recognises the importance of distinguishing between a complaint that is not upheld (because evidence does not support it) and a complaint that is deliberately false or malicious. Employees will not be penalised for raising a concern in good faith, even if it cannot be substantiated.

Verbal

Persistent suggestions to meet socially after refusal; unwelcome sexual advances or propositions; intrusive questions about a person’s sex or gender; suggestive remarks; gender-related insults; offensive comments about appearance or dress; innuendo or lewd comments; explicit discussion of own sex life.

Physical

Unwanted touching, hugging, kissing, or patting; invading personal space or blocking someone intimidatingly; sexual assault or coercive physical behaviour.

Non-verbal

Leering, whistling, sexually suggestive gestures; displaying offensive, pornographic, or inappropriate material.

Written or digital

Sending offensive, pornographic, or sexually suggestive material via text, email, video, social media, communication platforms or shared documents; posting inappropriate content online about a colleague.

Gossip or speculation

Spreading rumours or making derogatory comments about a person’s sexual orientation, gender identity, or alleged sexual behaviour.

Quid pro quo

Offering promotions, pay raises, or benefits in exchange for sexual favours; threatening demotion or negative treatment if sexual demands are refused.

Retaliation / Victimisation

Any adverse action taken against someone for reporting harassment or supporting a complainant.

2.5 Bullying

There is no legal definition of bullying. However, for the purposes of this policy, bullying is regarded as behaviour that is offensive, intimidating, malicious, insulting, or an abuse or misuse of power. It is often persistent, and has the effect, whether intended or perceived, of undermining, humiliating, or causing harm, emotionally or psychologically, to the recipient.

2.6 Examples of bullying

Bullying can take many forms, including physical, verbal, or non-verbal conduct. It is not limited to face-to-face interactions and may occur through email, phone calls, instant messaging, online platforms, or social media. While bullying may occur in the workplace, it can also take place outside of work, including during work-related activities, business travel, training events, or social functions connected to employment.

Bullying can affect anyone, regardless of their role or level within the organisation, and can be directed towards individuals or groups. Examples include (but are not limited to):

Verbal

Shouting, swearing, or aggressive language; persistent criticism; name-calling or belittling.

Physical

Pushing, hitting, or any form of physical intimidation; damaging someone’s property.

Psychological / Emotional

Ignoring or excluding someone; isolating them from work or social activities; setting unrealistic deadlines or workload to cause stress; undermining or deliberately sabotaging work.

Digital / Online

Sending threatening or abusive emails, texts, or messages; sharing humiliating content about someone online; cyberbullying on social media or messaging platforms.

Gossip or speculation

Spreading malicious rumours about someone’s personal life, work performance, or behaviour; making false or misleading statements intended to damage reputation; circulating private information without consent.

Abuse of power

Using authority to intimidate, control, or manipulate someone; blocking opportunities for promotion or training unfairly.

2.7 Discrimination

Discrimination occurs when an individual is treated unfairly or less favourably because of a protected characteristic, as defined under the Equality Act 2010 and listed under the harassment section of this policy. Discrimination can arise in many aspects of the workplace, including recruitment, training, promotion, performance management, dismissal, and day-to-day working relationships.

2.8 Examples of discrimination

There are several forms of discrimination under the Equality Act 2010:

Direct discrimination

Treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic.

Indirect discrimination

Applying a policy, practice, or rule that appears neutral but disproportionately disadvantages people with a protected characteristic, unless it can be objectively justified.

Discrimination arising from disability

Treating a disabled person unfavourably because of something connected with their disability, where such treatment cannot be justified.

Failure to make reasonable adjustments

Not making appropriate changes to remove barriers that place a disabled person at a substantial disadvantage compared to others.

By perception

Discriminating against someone because they are perceived to have a protected characteristic, even if that perception is incorrect.

By association

Discriminating against someone because of their association with a person who has a protected characteristic (e.g., a family member or partner).

2.9 Victimisation

Victimisation is defined under the Equality Act 2010 as treating someone unfairly or subjecting them to a detriment because they have:

made, or intend to make, a complaint or allegation of discrimination, harassment, or bullying

supported another person in making such a complaint (for example, by giving evidence or acting as a witness)

raised concerns about breaches of equality, diversity, or inclusion

Victimisation is unlawful, regardless of whether the original complaint is upheld, provided it was made in good faith.

The key factor is that victimisation occurs as a reaction to an individual exercising their rights under equality law. It can take many forms and may be overt or subtle. All workers are expected to treat colleagues who raise concerns with respect and professionalism, and to ensure they are not disadvantaged for doing so.
